steps.body:
The dot product also encodes the exact **angle** between vectors:

cos θ = (u · v) / (|u| |v|).

Divide the dot product by the product of magnitudes to get the cosine, then take arccos (recall). This one formula turns component arithmetic into geometry.
Zero dot product means a right angle. Watch it happen.

widget.prompt: u = (3, 4). Steer v until the dot product reads 0, then look at the angle.
widget.successFeedback: The angle snaps to 90°. That is what the dot product is FOR: one number that hits zero exactly when the arrows are perpendicular. And notice several v work — (4, −3), (−4, 3), (8, −6) — because perpendicular is a whole line of directions, not one arrow.
widget.lowFeedback: The dot product is negative, so the arrows lean AWAY from each other — the angle is past 90°. Swing v back toward u.
widget.highFeedback: The dot product is positive, so the arrows still lean the same way — the angle is under 90°. Swing v further from u.

cml.actionGoal: Change vector components and coordinate geometric movement with component and dot-product representations.

explanationVariants: The cosine √2/2 is the signature of 45°.

widget.prompt: For u = ⟨1, 0⟩, v = ⟨1, 1⟩, the angle θ between them is:

steps.body: When cos θ = 1 the vectors are **parallel** (same direction, 0°); when cos θ = −1 they're **antiparallel** (opposite, 180°). Parallel vectors are scalar multiples of each other, so their dot product equals the full product of magnitudes — no 'wasted' perpendicular part.

explanationVariants: Both point along the line y = x, so the angle between them is 0°.

commonErrors.feedback: Both lie along y = x — same direction. cos θ = 12/(2√2·3√2) = 1 → 0°.
These are PARALLEL (one is a scalar multiple of the other): angle 0°, not 90°.

explanationVariants: The vector ⟨1, √3⟩ points at 60° from the x-axis, so the angle to ⟨1,0⟩ is 60° — the cos θ = 1/2 signature.

commonErrors.feedback: cos θ = 1/2 → 60°. cos 45° = √2/2 ≈ 0.71, a different value.

explanationVariants: The 3-4-5 vector meets the x-axis at its own direction angle, 53.13°.

widget.prompt: Find the angle between ⟨3, 4⟩ and ⟨5, 0⟩, in degrees to two decimals.

commonErrors.feedback: 0.6 is the COSINE, not the angle. arccos(0.6) ≈ 53.13°.

takeaways: cos θ = (u · v)/(|u| |v|); then θ = arccos of that.
cos θ = 1 → parallel (0°); cos θ = −1 → antiparallel (180°); 0 → perpendicular.
steps.teaser: Final dot-product lesson: work done by a force.

concept.body: Angle between vectors: cos θ = (u·v)/(|u||v|), then θ = arccos. cos = 1 parallel, 0 perpendicular, −1 antiparallel.

commonErrors.feedback: Their dot product is 0, so cos θ = 0 → θ = 90°, not 0°.
